title: Arteris FlexGen Opens Up Multi-Die Traffic Management for Non-Coherent Networks
gist: Bernard Murphy explains that Arteris FlexGen Multi-Die extends traffic-management (bandwidth, latency, QoS) across chiplets for non-coherent NoCs by tunneling the NoC protocol through UCIe links, complementing last year's coherent Ncore Multi-Die. AMD is cited as an enthusiastic supporter and Arteris says it can use fewer UCIe ports than AXI-bridge approaches.

insights.claim: Hyperscalers and OEMs are building large systems on multi-chiplet architectures, in one case as many as 12 compute, fabric/cache and IO chiplets plus HBM, which require efficient traffic management between chiplets.
insights.speaker: Bernard Murphy
insights.so_what: Multi-chiplet scale-up is expanding the market for on-package interconnect IP.
insights.locator: Last year I wrote about Arteris

insights.claim: Beyond physical connectivity, multi-chiplet systems need traffic management of bandwidth, latency and quality of service across multiple traffic streams.
insights.speaker: Bernard Murphy
insights.so_what: QoS across dies becomes a design requirement, not an option.

insights.claim: Bridging a NoC to AXI and then to a UCIe connector works but does not preserve traffic policy management such as QoS across to the next chiplet, even though traffic management needs do not disappear at the chiplet edge.
insights.speaker: Bernard Murphy
insights.so_what: Standard AXI-to-UCIe bridging loses QoS, creating the gap FlexGen targets.
insights.locator: This is all good within a chiplet

insights.claim: Arteris Ncore Multi-Die addresses coherent traffic across chiplets, while non-coherent support is an even more common requirement, now addressed by FlexGen Multi-Die.
insights.speaker: Bernard Murphy
insights.so_what: Arteris now covers both coherent and non-coherent multi-die traffic, broadening its TAM.

insights.claim: FlexGen Multi-Die automatically tunnels the NoC protocol through the UCIe link, making the chiplet-to-chiplet interface transparent, whereas a designer would otherwise have to extract QoS information, send it as sideband signals and rebuild it on the other side.
insights.speaker: Bernard Murphy
insights.so_what: Automation removes a manual, error-prone integration step for chiplet designers.
insights.locator: A designer could of course handle this themselves

insights.claim: With FlexGen Multi-Die an architect can start from a monolithic design without committing which logic goes on which chiplet and experiment with partitioning options to see the QoS impact of die-to-die links.
insights.speaker: Bernard Murphy
insights.so_what: Early partitioning flexibility shortens chiplet architecture exploration.
insights.locator: This flexibility allows architects and designers

insights.claim: The solution is highly configurable and fairly agnostic to PHY IP, according to Arteris's Rick Bye, who says Arteris is already working with several companies with their own PHY IP, most notably AMD, which gave an enthusiastic endorsement; Arteris expects to qualify commercial UCIe IP options over time.
insights.speaker: Rick Bye
insights.so_what: AMD endorsement is a customer validation signal for Arteris.
insights.locator: Rick Bye, Director of Product Management and Marketing

insights.claim: If chiplets A and B both initiate and target traffic, FlexGen Multi-Die manages it up to bandwidth limits, whereas at least some AXI-to-UCI bridges require two UCIe ports on each chiplet, so FlexGen is more area, power and I/O efficient.
insights.speaker: Bernard Murphy
insights.so_what: Fewer UCIe ports save die area and power, a competitive argument for Arteris IP (vendor-side claim).
insights.locator: Another very interesting feature of the Arteris
